questions.q: Before the Maurya empire broke up, what post did Pushyamitra Shunga hold under the last Maurya emperor?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.118: the emperor was assassinated by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga. The other options are posts or roles that belong to other people or periods in the chapter.

questions.q: Which description fits many of the new kingdoms that emerged after the Maurya empire broke up?
questions.a: The chapter says the new kingdoms were often earlier tributary kingdoms under Maurya overlordship. Greek satraps and Central Asian tribes appear later and only in the northwest.
o: Often, they were earlier Maurya tributary kingdoms
They were colonies set up by Greek satraps in the south
They were provinces carved out by Ashoka's Dhamma
They were settlements of Central Asian tribes in Kalinga

questions.q: After the Maurya empire weakened, which region of the subcontinent was left exposed to invasions from outside?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.118: the northwest region became weak, exposing it to invasions from outside the subcontinent.

questions.q:
Statement I: Scholars call the period after the Mauryas the 'age of reorganisation' because existing regions were being reorganised into new, competing kingdoms.
Statement II: No new kingdoms arose in this period because the Shungas kept the Maurya empire intact.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Statement I is the chapter's own explanation of the name. Statement II is false: many new kingdoms emerged, and the Shunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire.
o: Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.

questions.q: Two neighbouring kings quarrel over a border district. Instead of fighting, one agrees to send his daughter to marry the other's son. Which method of gaining control does this show?
questions.a: A marriage between royal families to cement an alliance is exactly the book's 'matrimonial alliance', a peaceful method. Force is the other method the chapter names; the horse ritual and tolls are different ideas.

questions.q: King Devasena of a small kingdom moves most of his soldiers to the district where his land meets his neighbour's. Which statement from the chapter best explains his priority?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.120: there was constant wrestling for control over border areas because holding them kept the kingdom safe. The other options are not stated in the chapter.
o: Holding border areas kept the kingdom safe from attacks
Border areas held the richest farmland in the whole subcontinent
Border districts had to keep paying tribute to the Maurya emperor
Marriage alliances could only be signed at the border of kingdoms

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The period after the Mauryas is called the 'age of reorganisation'.
Reason (R): The northwest region became weak and was exposed to invasions from outside the subcontinent.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The name comes from existing regions being reorganised into new competing kingdoms, so the weakness of the northwest, though a real fact, does not explain the name.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the dynasties of this age.
1. The Shungas, Chedis and Satavahanas are dynasties from within the subcontinent.
2. The Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas are dynasties from outside the subcontinent.
3. The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas are dynasties from outside the subcontinent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 is false: the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas are listed with the Shungas, Chedis and Satavahanas as dynasties from within the subcontinent (Fig. 6.3, p.120).

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Pushyamitra Shunga  2. Matrimonial alliance  3. The northwest region  4. Reorganisation
Column B: a. Became weak and open to invasions  b. A peaceful way of gaining control  c. Assassinated the last Maurya emperor  d. Old regions made into new competing kingdoms
questions.a: Pushyamitra assassinated the last emperor; a marriage alliance is peaceful; the northwest became weak; reorganisation means regions remade into competing kingdoms.

questions.q: What is a matrimonial alliance? Give the example the chapter uses to explain it.
questions.a: An alliance arranged through a marriage, usually between two members of royal families. A king would offer his daughter in marriage into the royal family of a neighbouring kingdom to cement an alliance between the two kingdoms.
s: Defines it as an alliance arranged through marriage between royal families
Gives the daughter-married-into-neighbouring-royal-family example and its purpose of cementing the alliance

questions.q: (a) Name the two means by which the new kingdoms tried to gain control over neighbouring areas. (b) Why did kings fight hardest over border areas in particular?
questions.a: (a) Peaceful methods such as matrimonial alliances, and the use of force in warfare. (b) Controlling border areas was important to keep the kingdom safe from attacks.
s: Part (a): matrimonial alliances and warfare named
Part (b): border control kept the kingdom safe from attacks

questions.q: (a) Name any two dynasties from within the subcontinent. (b) The three dynasties from outside the subcontinent are the Indo-Greeks, the Shakas and the Kushanas. Which of them came originally from central Asia, and in which century CE did it probably enter India?
questions.a: (a) Any two of the Shungas, Chedis, Satavahanas, Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas. (b) The Kushanas, probably in the 2nd century CE.
s: Part (a): two correct dynasties from within the subcontinent
Part (b): Kushanas, 2nd century CE

questions.q: (a) In which century BCE does the year 185 BCE fall? (b) On a timeline running from 200 BCE to 300 CE, does 185 BCE lie before or after 100 BCE, and why?
questions.a: (a) The 2nd century BCE (200 BCE to 101 BCE). (b) Before 100 BCE, because BCE years count backwards: the larger the number, the earlier the year.
s: Part (a): 2nd century BCE
Part (b): earlier than 100 BCE, because BCE years count down towards CE

questions.q: Besides the political competition among kingdoms, name two developments that the chapter says happened together with it.
questions.a: A burst in the development of art, architecture and literature, and enriching cultural exchanges.
s: Names the growth of art, architecture and literature
Names the cultural exchanges

questions.q: Reena says, 'The last Maurya emperor was killed around 185 BCE, and the Shungas then took over all the lands the Mauryas had ruled.' Which part of her statement does the chapter support, and which part does it not?
questions.a: The first part is supported: the last emperor was assassinated around 185 BCE by Pushyamitra Shunga. The second part is not: the empire broke up, many new kingdoms emerged, and the Shunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire.
s: Verdict: partly right, the assassination around 185 BCE is supported
The empire broke up and many new kingdoms emerged
The Shunga empire was smaller, so they did not take over all Maurya lands

questions.q: A quiz answer reads: 'The Maurya empire broke up about 200 years after Ashoka.' Using the chapter, show that this cannot be correct.
questions.a: The chapter says the breakup came hardly half a century after Ashoka, that is about 50 years. 200 years is four times as long, so the answer contradicts the chapter.
s: Quotes the chapter: hardly half a century after Ashoka
Compares about 50 years with 200 years (four times as long)
Concludes the answer is wrong and corrects it

questions.q: Many of the new kingdoms had earlier been tributary kingdoms under Maurya overlordship. Explain how the breakup of the empire allowed such a kingdom to become independent, and how this explains why so many kingdoms appeared at about the same time.
questions.a: Once the last emperor was assassinated the empire broke up, so the overlord no longer controlled the tributary kingdoms. Each could stand alone as a new kingdom. Since the Maurya empire had many such tributaries, many new kingdoms appeared together and began to compete.
s: Breakup removes the Maurya overlordship
Tributary kingdoms become independent
Many tributaries therefore means many new competing kingdoms

questions.q: 'The Maurya empire broke up, but the subcontinent was not left in chaos: it was reorganised.' Justify this statement with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: The empire broke up after the last emperor was assassinated around 185 BCE. New kingdoms, many of them earlier tributary states, emerged and competed by marriage alliances or force, with border areas important for safety. Alongside, art, architecture and literature grew and cultural exchanges enriched life. The map changed, so the age is called one of reorganisation.
s: Cause: assassination around 185 BCE and breakup of the empire
New kingdoms, many of them former tributary states
Competition by matrimonial alliances or warfare, with border areas important
Growth of art, architecture, literature and cultural exchange
Concludes why 'reorganisation' fits better than 'collapse'

questions.q: Trace the chain of events from the assassination around 185 BCE to the arrival of outsiders in the subcontinent. Explain each link in the chain, and say through which part of the subcontinent the outsiders came.
questions.a: The last Maurya emperor was assassinated around 185 BCE by his commander-in-chief. The empire broke up and many new kingdoms emerged. The northwest region became weak. This exposed it to invasions from outside the subcontinent, so the Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas entered through the northwest frontier.
s: Assassination of the last emperor around 185 BCE
Breakup of the empire into many new kingdoms
Weakening of the northwest region
Exposure to invasions from outside
Outsiders (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas) enter by the northwest frontier

questions.q:
Anita's class has money for only one poster for the chapter's first Big Question, 'Why is the period after the Maurya empire called the age of reorganisation?'. Poster A shows the assassination around 185 BCE, the breakup and the new competing kingdoms. Poster B shows the weak northwest and the outsiders who entered it.
(a) What year do the first events on Poster A fall in, and in which century BCE is that?
(b) What happened to the northwest region, as Poster B must show?
(c) What two means did the new kingdoms use to compete, which Poster A should mention?
(d) Which poster answers the Big Question better, and what would you lose by not printing the other?
questions.a: (a) Around 185 BCE, in the 2nd century BCE. (b) It became weak, exposing it to invasions from outside the subcontinent. (c) Matrimonial alliances and warfare. (d) Poster A answers the question more directly because the name refers to regions being reorganised into new competing kingdoms; leaving out Poster B loses the reason outsiders could enter. A reasoned case for Poster B, as the cause of one big change in the map, is also acceptable.
s: Part (a): around 185 BCE, 2nd century BCE
Part (b): weak northwest exposed to invasion
Part (c): matrimonial alliances and warfare
Part (d): chooses a poster and names what the other would have added

questions.q:
King Veerasena's treasury holds 40 lakh rupees. His neighbour also claims a border district that guards Veerasena's own frontier. Plan 1: send his army of 4,000 to take the district, a season costing about 25 lakh rupees, against a neighbour's 6,000 soldiers. Plan 2: arrange a family link with the neighbour by offering his daughter in marriage; the gifts cost 8 lakh rupees, and the neighbour then promises not to attack the district, though Veerasena gives up one small border village.
(a) What does the book call the way of gaining control that Plan 2 uses, and Plan 1?
(b) How much of the treasury would be left under each plan?
(c) Why would the king care about holding the border district, according to the chapter?
(d) Which plan would you advise? Use your figures and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Plan 2 is a matrimonial alliance; Plan 1 is the use of force in warfare. (b) Plan 1: 40 - 25 = 15 lakh rupees. Plan 2: 40 - 8 = 32 lakh rupees. (c) Border areas are important for keeping the kingdom safe from attacks. (d) Plan 2 leaves 17 lakh rupees more, avoids fighting a larger army and still protects the district at the cost of one village; Plan 1 could win the whole district but is uncertain. A reasoned choice of Plan 1 is acceptable if it addresses the army sizes.
s: Part (a): matrimonial alliance and warfare
Part (b): 15 lakh and 32 lakh rupees
Part (c): border areas keep the kingdom safe
Part (d): decision using the figures and the chapter

questions.q: In the ashvamedha yajna, what is left to wander freely accompanied by soldiers?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.121: a horse accompanied by soldiers is left to wander. The bull (Nandi) appears later on Kushana coins and elephants on the Bharhut railings, which is where the confusion comes from.

questions.q: What did the Shungas do for Buddhist art at the Bharhut Stupa?
questions.a: The Karla caves belong to the Satavahanas, the headless statue to Kanishka and the Gandhara school to the Kushana age. The Shungas added the railings and reliefs (p.122).
o: They added carved railings and Buddha reliefs
They carved out the Karla caves for Buddhist monks
They set up the headless statue of a king there
They founded the Gandhara school of art

questions.q: Which language emerged as one of the preferred languages for philosophical and literary works in the Shunga period?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.122 names Sanskrit. Brahmi is a script, not a language; Greek and Tamil belong to other parts of the chapter.

questions.q:
Statement I: The Bharhut Stupa carries carvings of Lakshmi and of a group of singers and dancers.
Statement II: The Bharhut Stupa stands in present-day Odisha.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: The Bharhut Stupa is in present-day Madhya Pradesh. Odisha is where the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves of Kharavela are, a common mix-up.
o: Statement I is true and Statement II is false.
Statement I is false and Statement II is true.

questions.q: A visitor to Bharhut sees railings carved with scenes from the Buddha's life and says, 'The Shungas revived Vedic rituals, so they must have opposed Buddhist art.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says Vedic rituals revived but other schools of thought flourished, and the Shungas added the Buddhist reliefs. They also performed the ashvamedha, so a claim that they never performed any ritual is wrong too.
o: The Shungas revived Vedic rituals while other schools flourished
The Shungas supported only Vedic ideas, so Buddhist art stopped
The Bharhut carvings pre-date the Shungas, who added nothing
The Shungas never performed any Vedic ritual at all

questions.q: A king's ashvamedha horse crosses three neighbouring kingdoms without being stopped, but the ruler of a fourth kingdom seizes it. What does the ritual say happens next?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.121: if any ruler stopped the horse, it led to a battle to determine supremacy. Unchallenged territory was counted as part of the king's empire; stopping the horse does not give anything away.
o: A battle decides who is supreme
The fourth kingdom becomes a tributary
The king gives up the three lands he crossed
The horse is sent to Bharhut as an offering

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The reliefs and railings at the Bharhut Stupa are considered some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art.
Reason (R): The Shungas refused to patronise any art about the Buddha.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the chapter says the Shungas added railings and reliefs about the Buddha's life. R is false, because the Shungas patronised literature, art and architecture and other schools of thought flourished.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Shunga empire.
1. Pushyamitra's empire covered the whole subcontinent, just as the Maurya empire had.
2. Territory crossed unchallenged by the ashvamedha horse was considered part of the king's empire.
3. The Shunga empire was gone about a century after Pushyamitra.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the Shunga empire ruled parts of north and central India and was smaller than the Maurya empire. Statements 2 and 3 are in the chapter (p.121).

questions.q: Describe the ashvamedha yajna in your own words. How was a king's claim to supremacy decided in it?
questions.a: A Vedic ritual in which a horse accompanied by soldiers was left to wander freely. Territory it crossed unchallenged was considered part of the king's empire; if a ruler stopped the horse, a battle decided supremacy.
s: Horse with soldiers left to wander freely; territory crossed unchallenged becomes part of the empire
Stopping the horse leads to battle to decide supremacy

questions.q: (a) Who compiled the Yoga Sutras, and in which language were philosophical and literary works then often written? (b) Why does the chapter add that the period was not only about Vedic revival?
questions.a: (a) Patanjali; Sanskrit. (b) Other schools of thought continued to flourish alongside the revival of Vedic rituals.
s: Part (a): Patanjali and Sanskrit
Part (b): other schools of thought continued to flourish

questions.q: (a) State one thing Pushyamitra Shunga managed to do for his empire and one relationship he kept up with outsiders. (b) How long did the Shunga empire last after him?
questions.a: (a) He kept the empire safe from potential invaders and maintained friendly relations with the Greeks after some initial military campaign. (b) About a century; after that it was gone.
s: Part (a): kept the empire safe, and friendly with the Greeks after an initial campaign
Part (b): about a century

questions.q: The chapter's collage of Shunga art includes bronze bangles covered with a thin layer of gold, a comb of ivory and beads of a necklace. State two things historians can infer about the people of the time from these objects.
questions.a: Any two reasonable inferences: people wore jewellery and ornaments; craftsmen could work gold-plated bronze, ivory and beads; people cared about personal grooming; there was enough wealth and skill for fine craft. (Open inference: accept any two sensible points.)
s: First sensible inference from the objects
Second, different sensible inference

questions.q: The chapter says the Bharhut Stupa was 'probably built' in Ashoka's time, yet describes its railings and reliefs as Shunga art. Explain how both can be true, and why the reliefs matter for the history of art.
questions.a: The stupa itself was probably built earlier, in Ashoka's time; the Shungas later added the carved railings and reliefs of the Buddha's life. These reliefs are considered some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art.
s: Stupa built earlier; Shungas added railings and reliefs later
Reliefs are among the earliest examples of Buddhist art

questions.q: Imran says, 'Performing the ashvamedha yajna shows that Pushyamitra claimed to be the most powerful ruler, so he must have ruled the entire subcontinent.' Which part of this does the chapter support and which part not?
questions.a: The first part is supported: the ritual was performed to establish himself as the most powerful ruler. The second part is not: the Shunga empire covered parts of north and central India and was smaller than the Maurya empire.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supported: the ritual declares a king's position as most powerful
Not supported: only parts of north and central India, smaller than the Maurya empire

questions.q: Write a short story (four or five lines) of an ashvamedha horse that is stopped by one ruler. Make sure your story shows what the ritual says about the horse, about the lands it crosses and about the result of stopping it.
questions.a: A good story shows the horse wandering freely with soldiers, the lands crossed unchallenged counting as part of the king's empire, and the stopping of the horse leading to a battle to decide who is supreme.
s: Horse wanders freely with soldiers
Unchallenged lands treated as the king's empire
Stopping the horse leads to a battle for supremacy

questions.q: Say how the Shunga empire compared with the Maurya empire in size, state how long it lasted after Pushyamitra, and say how Pushyamitra dealt with the Greeks.
questions.a: It was smaller than the Maurya empire and was gone about a century after Pushyamitra. He kept it safe from invaders and kept friendly relations with the Greeks after some initial military campaign.
s: Smaller than the Maurya empire
Gone about a century after him
Initial campaign against the Greeks, then friendly relations

questions.q: 'The Shunga age revived old practices without shutting out new ones.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Vedic rituals such as the ashvamedha yajna were revived, but other schools of thought continued to flourish. The Shungas patronised literature, art and architecture. Sanskrit was preferred for philosophical and literary works and Patanjali compiled the Yoga Sutras. At Bharhut they added railings and reliefs of the Buddha's life, among the earliest examples of Buddhist art.
s: Revival of Vedic rituals with the ashvamedha as example
Other schools of thought still flourished
Sanskrit works and the Yoga Sutras
Bharhut railings and reliefs as Buddhist art
Draws the conclusion that revival and openness went together

questions.q: Explain what Pushyamitra Shunga achieved and where his rule fell short. Refer to the dynasty he founded, the ritual he performed, his dealings with the Greeks, and the fate of the empire.
questions.a: He founded the Shunga dynasty ruling parts of north and central India and performed the ashvamedha yajna to establish himself as the most powerful ruler. He kept the empire safe from invaders and kept friendly relations with the Greeks after an initial campaign. But his empire was smaller than the Maurya empire and was gone a century later.
s: Founded the dynasty over parts of north and central India
Performed the ashvamedha yajna to declare his position
Kept the empire safe and made peace with the Greeks after a campaign
Empire smaller than the Maurya empire
Gone a century later, so limited lasting success

questions.q:
A guide at the Bharhut Stupa in Madhya Pradesh tells 36 students of Class 7, 'This stupa was probably built in the time of Ashoka, and a later dynasty then enriched it. All the carvings you see show only the Buddha's life.' The school has Rs 12,000 for the outing. A bus visit costs Rs 450 per student; a photograph-study session in class, covering every panel, costs Rs 9,000 for all 36.
(a) Which dynasty enriched the stupa, and what did it add?
(b) Why are these additions important for the history of art?
(c) Name two carvings from the chapter that show the guide's last sentence is not accurate.
(d) Work out how many students the bus visit can take within the Rs 12,000 and compare it with the photograph session. Advise the school, giving one reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Shungas; carved railings and reliefs about the Buddha's life. (b) They are considered some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art. (c) Any two of Lakshmi, singers and dancers, elephants holding the wheel of dharma. (d) 12,000 / 450 = 26 students (26 x 450 = 11,700), 10 fewer than the class; the session reaches all 36 for Rs 9,000. A justified choice is accepted: the session shows every panel to everyone, while the visit shows the real railings to 26.
s: Part (a): Shungas, railings and reliefs
Part (b): earliest examples of Buddhist art
Part (c): two carvings that are not scenes of the Buddha's life
Part (d): 26 students against all 36, with a justified choice

questions.q:
Rajat is making a poster on Pushyamitra Shunga, who took power around 185 BCE. He must choose the title for the Shunga dynasty: 'Protector of a smaller empire' or 'Patron of art and learning'.
(a) According to the chapter, how long did the Shunga empire last after him, and so by about which year BCE was it gone?
(b) Which Vedic ritual did Pushyamitra perform, and what was it meant to show?
(c) What does the chapter say about his dealings with the Greeks?
(d) Name two pieces of evidence of patronage from the chapter, and say which title you would pick.
questions.a: (a) About a century; 185 - 100 = about 85 BCE. (b) The ashvamedha yajna, to establish himself as the most powerful ruler. (c) After some initial military campaign he maintained friendly relations, and he kept his empire safe from potential invaders. (d) Patronage: literature (Sanskrit works, Yoga Sutras) and the Bharhut railings and reliefs. Either title is defensible: 'Protector' rests on safety and friendly relations; 'Patron' rests on the art and learning, but it describes the dynasty and not only him.
s: Part (a): about a century, so about 85 BCE
Part (b): ashvamedha yajna to declare supremacy
Part (c): initial campaign, then friendly relations; kept the empire safe
Part (d): two evidences of patronage and a justified title

questions.q: The Satavahanas are sometimes referred to by which other name?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.124 says they are sometimes referred to as 'Andhras'. 'Keralaputra' is the Chera name (p.133), 'devaputra' (son of God) is part of Kanishka's title (p.136), and bhikshu-raja is Kharavela's title (p.128).

questions.q: Many Satavahana coins show a ship with two masts. What does the chapter say this suggests?
questions.a: The chapter says ships on coins suggest maritime trade was important, and the type of ship suggests advanced shipbuilding and navigation. The other options are not claimed by the book.
o: Maritime trade was important to the economy
Tolls were collected only at the sea ports of the coast
Agriculture in their land had failed and trade replaced it
Their kings were trained as sailors and ship captains

questions.q:
Statement I: Satavahana princes were never named after their mothers; they always took their fathers' names.
Statement II: Gautamiputra Satakarni was named after his mother, Gautami Balashri.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.126: princes were often named after their mothers, with Gautamiputra Satakarni as the example. The words 'never' and 'always' make Statement I false.
o: Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.

questions.q: To which group of people did Satavahana kings often grant tax-free agricultural land?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.127: they were followers of Vasudeva yet gave tax-free land to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks. The 'only' options narrow a list the book gives in full.
o: Vedic scholars and Jaina and Buddhist monks
Only Vedic scholars, as followers of Vasudeva
Only Buddhist monks, as at the Karla caves
Traders stationed at the toll posts near Pune

questions.q: Archaeologists dig up Satavahana coins in Gujarat and also in Andhra Pradesh. Which conclusion does the chapter support?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.125 says the coins have been found from Gujarat to Andhra Pradesh, India's western and eastern coasts. That supports wide circulation, not a shift of capital or Roman minting.
o: Their coins circulated across both coasts
The capital shifted from Gujarat to Andhra Pradesh
The Shungas ruled both coasts at that same time
Roman traders minted the coins for the kings

questions.q: A trader driving carts near Pune stops at a cave on the trade route where officials collect tolls and merchants rest. Which site fits this description in the chapter?
questions.a: The Naneghat caves lay close to a major trade route and were used for collection of tolls and taxes and as resting places for traders. Karla was made for Buddhist monks, Pitalkhora has the yaksha, and Udayagiri is in Kalinga.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Literature, art and culture received significant contributions in the Satavahana kingdom.
Reason (R): Economic prosperity and a relatively peaceful political period made such development possible.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the chapter says prosperity and relative peace facilitated the development of literature, art and culture.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Satavahanas.
1. Coins with ships on them point to the importance of maritime trade.
2. Farming in the Krishna-Godavari river system played no part in the kingdom's economic stability.
3. Weak central control and a gradual economic decline helped break the empire into smaller kingdoms in the 3rd century CE.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: agriculture in the Krishna-Godavari system gave economic stability. Statements 1 and 3 are in the chapter (pp.125, 127-128).

questions.q:
Match each site or object in Column A with the fact in Column B.
Column A: 1. Naneghat caves  2. Karla caves  3. Pitalkhora yaksha  4. Inscription at Nashik
Column B: a. Made by a goldsmith  b. Cut for Buddhist monks near Lonavala  c. Carved for a queen who donated land to monks  d. Near a trade route; tolls collected
questions.a: Naneghat: tolls near a trade route; Karla: Buddhist monks near Lonavala; Pitalkhora yaksha: goldsmith Kanhadasa; Nashik inscription: Gautami Balashri.

questions.q: (a) Agriculture in which river system gave the Satavahana kingdom economic stability? (b) Name one import the chapter names and one of the goods exchanged with the Roman Empire, and say what tolls and taxes on such trade gave the kingdom.
questions.a: (a) The Krishna-Godavari river system. (b) An import such as glass or perfumed ointments, and a good such as spices, textiles, sandalwood or ivory; tolls and taxes added revenue to the kingdom.
s: Part (a): Krishna-Godavari river system
Part (b): one import, one traded good and revenue from tolls and taxes

questions.q: (a) Who was Gautami Balashri, and what did she donate? (b) What does the inscription she had carved at Nashik show about her?
questions.a: (a) A powerful Satavahana queen, the mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni, who donated land to Buddhist monks. (b) It shows her influence in the kingdom.
s: Part (a): queen and mother of Gautamiputra; land to Buddhist monks
Part (b): the inscription shows her influence

questions.q: Where were the Naneghat caves located, and what were they used for?
questions.a: They were near Pune, close to a major trade route. They were used for collection of tolls and taxes and as resting places for traders.
s: Located near Pune, close to a major trade route
Used for tolls and taxes and as resting places for traders

questions.q: The yaksha from Pitalkhora carries the words 'made by Kanhadasa, a goldsmith'. What does this tell us, and what question does it raise about professions at the time?
questions.a: A goldsmith made a stone sculpture, so a craftsman who worked in metal also carved stone. The chapter leaves this as a question to think about: a reasonable inference is that professions were not as fixed as we may think or that skills overlapped, and any sensible inference should be credited.
s: Reads the inscription: a goldsmith carved the stone sculpture
Infers that crafts or professions overlapped or were not rigid

questions.q: Give two ways in which the Satavahana kings supported schools of thought other than their own devotion to Vasudeva.
questions.a: They granted tax-free agricultural land to Vedic scholars and to Jaina and Buddhist monks, and they contributed to the Karla caves made for Buddhist monks.
s: Tax-free land to scholars and monks of different schools
A second example such as the Karla caves for Buddhist monks

questions.q: Meera says, 'Satavahana kings gave tax-free land only to Buddhist monks, because they built the Karla caves for them.' Zoya says, 'They gave it to scholars and monks of several schools.' Whose view does the chapter support, and why?
questions.a: Zoya's. The kings, though followers of Vasudeva, often granted tax-free agricultural land to Vedic scholars and to Jaina and Buddhist monks. The Karla caves were made for Buddhist monks, but that does not limit the land grants to them.
s: Verdict: Zoya's view
Land grants went to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks
Karla caves for Buddhist monks do not show an 'only' for the land grants

questions.q: How can historians know that the Satavahana kingdom traded far beyond its borders? Name three kinds of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Coins with ships found from Gujarat to Andhra Pradesh, the Naneghat caves with their tolls on a trade route, and the record of goods exported to and imported from the Roman Empire such as spices and glass.
s: Ship coins found along both coasts
Naneghat caves used for tolls and taxes
Goods traded with the Roman Empire

questions.q: The Naneghat inscriptions in Brahmi script contain some numerals. What does the chapter say about the origin of modern numerals, and what do the inscriptions tell us about the widow queen?
questions.a: Some Brahmi numerals resemble today's shapes, one of many evidences that modern numerals originated in India. The queen performed several Vedic rituals, including the ashvamedha yajna, and made donations of land, cows, horses, elephants and silver coins.
s: Numerals resemble modern ones; origin in India
Vedic rituals including the ashvamedha
Donations such as land, cows, horses, elephants, silver coins

questions.q: 'The Satavahana kingdom's prosperity rested on trade.' Justify this statement with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Coins with ships were found from Gujarat to Andhra Pradesh and show maritime trade and advanced shipbuilding. Goods such as spices, textiles, sandalwood and ivory went out and glass and ointments came in, reaching the Roman Empire. Tolls and taxes added revenue, collected for example at the Naneghat caves. Farming in the Krishna-Godavari system gave stability as well. Prosperity and peace then supported literature, art and culture.
s: Ship coins across both coasts
Exports and imports with the Roman Empire
Tolls and taxes, Naneghat caves
Agriculture in the Krishna-Godavari system as the other base
Prosperity leading to art and culture

questions.q: The Satavahana kingdom left behind coins, cave sites and inscriptions. Choose the ONE kind of source you think tells a historian most about life in the kingdom (not only trade) and defend your choice with three pieces of evidence from the chapter. Then say what one other kind of source adds.
questions.a: A strong answer chooses one source and supports it. For example, inscriptions: the Nashik inscription of Gautami Balashri shows a powerful queen who donated land to Buddhist monks; the Naneghat inscriptions show a widow queen performing Vedic rituals including the ashvamedha and giving land, cows, horses and silver coins; the Brahmi numerals show early number symbols. Coins add the evidence of ships and maritime trade, and caves like Karla and Naneghat add patronage and toll collection. Accept any consistent choice.
s: Chooses one kind of source
First piece of evidence from the chapter
Second piece of evidence
Third piece of evidence
What another kind of source adds

questions.q:
Class 7 plans a 'Satavahana trade fair' for 300 visitors in 2 hours. The goods on the table are sandalwood, glass, ivory, perfumed ointments, textiles and spices. The class has Rs 3,000 for one display idea. Idea 1: a model of a cave on a trade route with a toll-counter game for 25 visitors at a time, 10 minutes a round, costing Rs 2,100. Idea 2: 30 replica coins with a two-masted ship, at Rs 85 each, one for each of the first 30 visitors.
(a) Which goods does the chapter name as imports, and which as exchanged with the Roman Empire? Sort the six goods.
(b) Which actual cave near Pune does Idea 1 copy, and what was it used for?
(c) What does a ship on a Satavahana coin suggest?
(d) Work out the money left over under each idea and how many visitors each idea reaches in the 2 hours. Advise the class, giving a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Imports: glass and perfumed ointments. Exchanged goods: sandalwood, ivory, textiles, spices. (b) The Naneghat caves, used for collecting tolls and taxes and as resting places for traders. (c) That maritime trade was important. (d) Idea 1 leaves 3,000 - 2,100 = Rs 900; 120 minutes / 10 = 12 rounds x 25 = 300 visitors. Idea 2 costs 30 x 85 = Rs 2,550, leaves Rs 450 and reaches 30 visitors. Idea 1 reaches all visitors and shows tolls; Idea 2 gives direct evidence of sea trade but only to 30. A justified choice is accepted.
s: Part (a): two imports and four exchanged goods sorted
Part (b): Naneghat caves, tolls and taxes, resting places
Part (c): maritime trade was important
Part (d): Rs 900 and Rs 450, 300 against 30 visitors, justified advice

questions.q:
A teachers' committee must choose one source for a display called 'Royal women as patrons'. Source 1 is an inscription at Nashik that a queen mother had carved, after whom her son, a prince, was named. Source 2 is a set of inscriptions in caves near Pune about a widow queen, in Brahmi script, listing gods and gifts.
(a) Why was the prince in Source 1 known by his mother's name, and what was his name?
(b) What had the queen in Source 1 donated?
(c) Name the Vedic ritual and two gods mentioned in the Source 2 inscriptions, and the kinds of people who received her gifts.
(d) The display is about patronage of many groups. Which source fits better, and what does the other source still add?
questions.a: (a) Princes were often named after their mothers; Gautamiputra Satakarni, son of Gautami Balashri. (b) Land to Buddhist monks. (c) The ashvamedha yajna (among several Vedic rituals); gods such as Indra, Chandra and Surya; gifts to priests, guests, workers, scholars and monks. (d) Source 2 fits better because her gifts went to priests, guests, workers, scholars and monks, so many groups; Source 1 still adds the naming custom and her support of Buddhist monks, and shows the Nashik inscription's evidence of influence.
s: Part (a): naming custom and Gautamiputra Satakarni
Part (b): land to Buddhist monks
Part (c): ashvamedha, two gods, and recipients of the gifts
Part (d): Source 2 with reason, and what Source 1 still adds

questions.q: Near which city are the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves of the Chedi period found?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.128 places them near Bhubaneswar. Pune (Naneghat), Vidisha (the Heliodorus pillar) and Lonavala (Karla) are other sites in the same chapter.

questions.q: What does the Hathigumpha inscription record year after year?
questions.a: The chapter says it records Kharavela's victorious military campaigns and his benevolent works for the welfare of his people (p.129). The other options belong to Karikala, the Satavahanas and Patanjali.
o: A king's victories and welfare works
Karikala's irrigation works on the Kaveri
The tolls collected on a trade route near Pune
The Yoga Sutras compiled in a reign

questions.q: Which statement about Kharavela's attitude to other schools of thought does the chapter support?
questions.a: The chapter calls him a devoted follower of Jain teachings who respected all schools; the inscription calls him a respector of every sect and repairer of every temple. The 'only' options narrow what the book says.
o: He followed Jain teachings yet respected all sects
He gave support only to Jain monks of his own faith
He set aside all other schools to protect Jain teachings
He built cave monasteries only for Buddhist monks

questions.q: The title 'bhikshu-raja' given to Kharavela means
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.128: he was sometimes called bhikshu-raja or monk-king. 'King of kings' and 'son of God' are parts of Kanishka's title and 'crowned kings' is how the Sangams refer to the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas.

questions.q: Archaeologists find a hillside monastery with panels, statues and large rooms, all carved out of the living rock near Bhubaneswar and probably made for Jain monks. Which style of architecture does it show?
questions.a: The chapter calls the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves notable examples of rock-cut architecture. Bharhut railings, Gandhara and Mathura are other art forms in the chapter.
o: Stupa railing art as at Bharhut

questions.q: Pooja reads that Kharavela defeated an alliance of south Indian kings and concludes he ruled the far south. What caution does the chapter give her?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.129: the location of that battle is unknown and he does not seem to have invaded the southern region. Ashoka's empire stopped at the southern kingdoms, so a claim that Ashoka had conquered the whole south is also false.
o: The Cholas ruled all of Kalinga at the time
Ashoka had already conquered the whole south
Kharavela's inscription is written in Greek script

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After the Maurya empire declined, Kalinga stayed a weak region with no ruler of note.
Reason (R): Kalinga rose as a prominent power under the kings of the Chedi dynasty.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false and R is true: the chapter says Kalinga rose as a prominent power after the Mauryas under the Chedis, with Kharavela as one of their main rulers.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about Kharavela and his age.
1. Kharavela is sometimes called the monk-king.
2. The Hathigumpha inscription mentions a council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions.
3. The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves were likely developed for Jain monks.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are in the chapter (pp.128-129): the title bhikshu-raja, the council from a hundred regions, and the caves likely made for Jain monks.

questions.q: (a) In which script is the Hathigumpha inscription written? (b) Name the two kinds of achievement of Kharavela that it records.
questions.a: (a) Brahmi script. (b) His victorious military campaigns and his benevolent works for the welfare of his people.
s: Part (a): Brahmi
Part (b): campaigns and welfare works

questions.q: What features of the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves make them examples of rock-cut architecture?
questions.a: They have intricate panels and statues and spacious rooms carved into the rock itself, showing the skill of the craftsmen.
s: Panels and statues carved into the rock
Spacious rooms cut out of the rock, showing craftsmen's skill

questions.q: (a) Quote two descriptions Kharavela gives of himself in the inscription. (b) What does the chapter say such a claim shows about a ruler's role in India?
questions.a: (a) For example 'accomplished in extraordinary virtues' and 'respector of every sect and repairer of every temple'. (b) A ruler takes pride in extending protection to all schools of thought, which is part of what may be called the Indian ethos.
s: Part (a): two correct descriptions
Part (b): protection of all schools of thought as part of the Indian ethos

questions.q: (a) Which earlier war in Kalinga does the chapter ask you to remember? (b) After the decline of what did Kalinga rise as a power?
questions.a: (a) The Kalinga war mentioned in the previous chapter (Ashoka's war). (b) After the decline of the Maurya empire, under the Chedi dynasty.
s: Part (a): the Kalinga war of the previous chapter
Part (b): the decline of the Maurya empire, Chedi dynasty

questions.q: (a) How does the chapter describe the regularity of the rock-cut chambers at Udayagiri-Khandagiri? (b) Which two tools does it suggest the artisans may have used to achieve it?
questions.a: (a) The chambers are very regular, sculpted nearly two millennia ago. (b) A chisel and a hammer.
s: Part (a): regular chambers sculpted nearly two thousand years ago
Part (b): chisel and hammer

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'Kharavela was called the monk-king, so he gave up ruling and lived only as a monk.' Which part of this is supported by the chapter, and which part is not?
questions.a: Supported: he was a devoted follower of Jain teachings and was sometimes called bhikshu-raja, the monk-king. Not supported: he did not give up ruling; the Hathigumpha inscription records his victorious campaigns and welfare works year after year, and he respected all schools.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supported: devoted Jain, called the monk-king
Not supported: campaigns and welfare works show he ruled actively

questions.q: The Hathigumpha inscription records Kharavela's achievements 'year after year'. What does this phrase tell a historian about how the record was made, and which two kinds of event does it list?
questions.a: It suggests the record was kept as a sequence, one year's deeds after another, so it can be read as a list of events in order. It lists his victorious military campaigns and his benevolent works for the welfare of his people.
s: Records are arranged year after year, in a sequence
Victorious military campaigns
Welfare works for his people

questions.q: Write a three-sentence script for a guide at Udayagiri-Khandagiri. Your script must say for whom the caves were likely made, what they show about the craftsmen, and what the Hathigumpha inscription tells us.
questions.a: The caves were likely developed for Jain monks. Their panels, statues and rooms cut into rock show the great skill of the craftsmen and are examples of rock-cut architecture. The Hathigumpha inscription in Brahmi records Kharavela's victories and welfare works year after year.
s: Caves for Jain monks
Craftsmen's skill and rock-cut architecture
Inscription records campaigns and welfare works

questions.q: Describe how Kalinga rose to power after the Mauryas. In your answer connect the earlier Kalinga war, the decline of the Maurya empire, the Chedi dynasty, Kharavela's faith and the caves near Bhubaneswar.
questions.a: The chapter asks us to remember the Kalinga war of the previous chapter. After the Maurya empire declined, Kalinga rose as a prominent power under the Chedi dynasty. Kharavela was one of their main rulers, a devoted follower of Jain teachings who respected all schools. Near Bhubaneswar the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves, likely developed for Jain monks, show the rock-cut skill of craftsmen.
s: Kalinga war of the previous chapter recalled
Rise after the decline of the Maurya empire
Chedi dynasty with Kharavela as a main ruler
His Jain faith and respect for all schools
Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves for Jain monks

questions.q: Your class is nominating Kharavela for a 'ruler who protected every faith' award. Write a nomination of five points using evidence from the chapter. Include one point that a critic could use to argue against the nomination and say how you would answer it.
questions.a: Points: devoted Jain who respected all schools; calls himself respector of every sect and repairer of every temple; created a council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions; caves for monks; Hathigumpha inscription proudly records protection of all schools of thought. A critic may say that he was a Jain and a conqueror; the reply is that the inscription shows his protection extended beyond his own faith.
s: First point: respected all schools despite Jain devotion
Second point: respector of every sect and repairer of every temple
Third point: council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions
Fourth point: caves or inscription as record
A critic's objection and a reply

questions.q:
A class of 45 students visits Bhubaneswar for two hours, 120 minutes, at the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves. The guide says that a cave there prominently displays a famous inscription. Plan A: spend 20 minutes at each of 5 caves, including the inscription cave. Plan B: spend 60 minutes at the inscription cave and 15 minutes at each of 4 other caves.
(a) For whom were these caves likely developed?
(b) Name the inscription and the script in which it is written.
(c) Check whether both plans fit exactly into the 120 minutes.
(d) Which plan would you choose for this class, and why? Refer to what the inscription records.
questions.a: (a) Jain monks. (b) The Hathigumpha inscription, in Brahmi script. (c) Plan A: 5 x 20 = 100 minutes, 20 minutes short of the time; Plan B: 60 + 4 x 15 = 120 minutes, exactly. (d) Either is acceptable if justified: Plan B gives time to read about his campaigns, welfare works and respect for every sect; Plan A shows more caves and the range of rock-cut work.
s: Part (a): Jain monks
Part (b): Hathigumpha inscription, Brahmi
Part (c): 100 minutes against exactly 120 minutes
Part (d): plan chosen with reference to the inscription

questions.q:
Maya is writing one line for a class timeline on Kharavela. Her notes say: (i) he claims to have defeated an alliance of south Indian kings; (ii) Ashoka's own empire stopped at the southern kingdoms; (iii) the chapter says he states that he gets hundreds of pearls brought from a southern kingdom.
(a) What does the chapter say about where the claimed battle took place and whether he invaded the south?
(b) What does note (ii) tell us about the southern kingdoms in Maurya times?
(c) Which southern kingdom is the source of the pearls in note (iii)?
(d) Do notes (i) and (iii) together suggest that Kalinga's dealings with the south were mainly conflict or mainly contact? Give a reasoned judgement.
questions.a: (a) The location is unknown and he does not seem to have invaded the south. (b) They stayed independent even at the height of Maurya power. (c) The Pandya kingdom. (d) Either answer is acceptable if reasoned: the battle claim suggests conflict, though unverified; pearls brought from the Pandyas suggest trade contact, which his own inscription states; a balanced answer notes both.
s: Part (a): location unknown, no invasion of the south
Part (b): the south stayed independent
Part (c): the Pandya kingdom
Part (d): a reasoned judgement using both notes

questions.q: The word 'sangam' is derived from the Sanskrit 'sangha'. In the chapter's context it refers to
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.130: sangam means 'association' or 'coming together', here an assembly of the poets. A council of kings is the tempting wrong idea; the word does not name a political body.
o: a council of kings and ministers

questions.q: What does Sangam poetry mainly express?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.130: it expresses personal emotions such as love and societal values like heroism and generosity. The other options are things recorded in inscriptions or about other rulers in the chapter.
o: The gifts of a Satavahana widow queen
The ways of building the Kallanai

questions.q:
Statement I: The Kallanai has been restored several times and is still in use.
Statement II: By diverting Kaveri water, it brought more land under cultivation and earned the delta the name 'rice bowl of the South'.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Both are from p.132: the Grand Anicut was restored several times, is still used for irrigation, and made the delta the rice bowl of the South.
o: Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.

questions.q: Which of these was the capital of the Pandyas?
questions.a: Chapter 6 pp.131-133: Vanji was the Chera capital, Puhar (Kaveripattinam) the Chola capital city in the Silappadikaram, and Pratishthana a Satavahana capital. Madurai is the Pandya capital.

questions.q: A merchant from the Roman Empire asks, 'Which southern kingdom is described in your chapter as a hub for the export of spices, timber, ivory and pearls?' Which answer is correct?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.133 says the Chera kingdom became a hub for export of spices, timber, ivory and pearls. The Pandyas are noted for pearls and naval power, the Cholas for the Kallanai, and the Satavahanas are a Deccan dynasty.
o: The Pandyas, the pearl and naval kingdom
The Cholas, the kingdom of the Kallanai

questions.q: A guide in Chennai tells a story: a woman proves her husband's innocence by showing her second anklet, and a city is destroyed after her curse. Which text is she describing?
questions.a: This is the tale of Kannagi in the Silappadikaram, composed soon after the Sangam collections. The Hathigumpha inscription is Kharavela's record; Indika mentions the Pandyas, not this tale.
o: A Sangam anthology of love poems

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Silappadikaram centres on the principles of justice and the ruler's dharma to protect it.
Reason (R): Kannagi is worshipped even today in Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The epic's theme is justice and the ruler's duty; the worship of Kannagi today is a separate fact and does not explain why the story is about justice.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the three southern kingdoms.
1. The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas often competed with each other for control over the South.
2. The Cheras ruled the eastern coast of Tamil Nadu with their capital at Madurai.
3. The Cholas ruled parts of south India only until the 3rd century CE.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is true (p.129). Statement 2 is false: the Cheras ruled western Tamil Nadu and Kerala from Vanji. Statement 3 is false: the Cholas ruled from the 3rd century BCE to the 13th century CE (p.130).

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kallanai  2. Silappadikaram  3. Cheras  4. Pandyas
Column B: a. Known for pearls and naval power  b. Diverts Kaveri water to the delta  c. Keralaputra, a hub for exports  d. The tale of the anklet
questions.a: Kallanai: water diversion; Silappadikaram: tale of the anklet; Cheras (Keralaputra): export hub; Pandyas: pearls and naval power.

questions.q: (a) Who built the Kallanai, and from which river does it divert water? (b) How did it earn the Kaveri delta the name 'rice bowl of the South'?
questions.a: (a) Karikala; the Kaveri. (b) It helped bring more land under cultivation in the central and southern parts of the delta.
s: Part (a): Karikala and the Kaveri
Part (b): more land brought under cultivation in the delta

questions.q: What is Sangam literature? Why do historians consult it much?
questions.a: Several collections or anthologies of poems, the oldest literature in south India, composed by poets of the Sangam Age. Historians consult it to investigate the society and culture of the times.
s: Anthologies of poems, the oldest in south India
Historians use it to study society and culture

questions.q: (a) Name the capital cities of the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas. (b) In the Silappadikaram, which of these cities was cursed by Kannagi, and in whose kingdom was she finally honoured as a goddess?
questions.a: (a) Puhar (Kaveripattinam) or Uraiyur for the Cholas, Vanji for the Cheras, Madurai for the Pandyas. (b) Madurai was cursed; she was honoured in the Chera kingdom.
s: Part (a): the three capitals
Part (b): Madurai cursed, Chera kingdom honours her

questions.q: Give two reasons why the Chera kingdom became a hub of trade.
questions.a: It had extensive trade connections with the Roman Empire and West Asia, and it exported goods such as spices, timber, ivory and pearls.
s: Trade connections with the Roman Empire and West Asia
Export of spices, timber, ivory and pearls

questions.q: (a) In his work Indika, which writer mentions the Pandya kingdom, and what does he say about it? (b) What did Kharavela say about pearls and the Pandya kingdom?
questions.a: (a) Megasthenes; the kingdom was prosperous, with a strong administration and active trade with the Greeks and Romans. (b) He states that he gets hundreds of pearls brought from the Pandya kingdom.
s: Part (a): Megasthenes, prosperous and well administered
Part (b): hundreds of pearls brought from the Pandya kingdom

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Ashoka's edicts name the Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms, so they were part of his empire.' Bhavna says, 'The edicts name them because his empire stopped at them.' Whose reading does the chapter support, and what does it conclude about the southern kingdoms?
questions.a: Bhavna's. The chapter says Ashoka's empire stopped at those south Indian kingdoms, which he mentions in his edicts. This suggests they remained independent even at the height of Maurya power.
s: Verdict: Bhavna's reading
Ashoka's empire stopped at those kingdoms and his edicts mention them
They remained independent even at the height of Maurya power

questions.q: A student writes, 'The Sangam Age lasted for only about a hundred years.' Use the dates in the chapter to show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter dates the rise of the three kingdoms from the 2nd or 3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE. Even if it began in the last year of the 2nd century BCE and ended in the first year of the 3rd century CE, that is about 100 + 200 = 300 years, three times the claim.
s: Quotes the chapter's dates
Works out a minimum of about 300 years
Concludes that a hundred years is too short

questions.q: The Silappadikaram centres on justice and a ruler's dharma. Which events in the story show a ruler failing in that dharma and then facing the result?
questions.a: The Pandya king had Kovalan executed on a false charge of theft. Kannagi proved his innocence by revealing her second anklet. The king, realising his mistake, died of shock.
s: Kovalan falsely accused and executed
Kannagi proves innocence with the second anklet
The king realises his mistake and dies of shock

questions.q: 'The Kallanai shows a ruler's concern for his people.' Justify this statement with details from the chapter, and add one more example of a southern ruling family showing such concern.
questions.a: Karikala built the Kallanai, a water-diversion system just downstream of the Srirangam island, to divert Kaveri water to central and southern parts of the delta. More land came under cultivation, earning the name rice bowl of the South. Restored several times, it still helps millions of people in Tamil Nadu. The Pandyas left inscriptions asserting great concern for their subjects' welfare and encouraging all schools of thought.
s: Karikala built the Kallanai on the Kaveri
Diverts water to the delta, more cultivation, rice bowl of the South
Restored several times and still used
Benefit to millions in Tamil Nadu
A second example: Pandya inscriptions on subjects' welfare

questions.q: The Silappadikaram takes Kannagi through three kingdoms. Trace her story kingdom by kingdom and explain what each place shows about justice and the ruler's dharma.
questions.a: Kannagi lived happily with Kovalan in the prosperous Chola capital, Puhar, until Kovalan lost his wealth. They went to Madurai, the Pandya capital, where Kovalan was falsely accused of theft and executed by the king. Kannagi proved his innocence with her second anklet; the king died of shock and she cursed Madurai, which the god of fire destroyed. She walked west to the Chera kingdom, where she was honoured as a goddess. The epic centres on the principles of justice and the ruler's dharma to protect it.
s: Chola capital Puhar: life before the loss
Madurai: false accusation and execution of Kovalan
Second anklet proves innocence, the king dies of shock, Madurai is cursed
Chera kingdom honours her as a goddess
Links to justice and the ruler's dharma

questions.q:
In a class trading game, a ship from the kingdom of the 'sons of Kerala' carries 240 units of cargo to Roman buyers: 40% spices, 25% timber, 20% ivory and the rest pearls. The teacher can add one more card to the board, and wants it to be about the good the ship carries the least of.
(a) Name the dynasty and its capital.
(b) How many units of each good does the ship carry, and which good is the least?
(c) Which other southern kingdom is described as famous for that good, and for what else?
(d) The teacher also considers a card on the Chera trade with Rome instead. Which card would you add, and why? Use the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Cheras (Keralaputra), capital Vanji, present-day Karur. (b) Spices 96, timber 60, ivory 48, pearls 36; pearls are least. (c) The Pandyas, famous for pearls and as a naval power. (d) The Pandya card follows the teacher's rule and adds a new kingdom; the Chera trade card repeats the ship's story. A justified choice of the Rome card is accepted if it argues the ship's story needs one more fact.
s: Part (a): Cheras, Vanji
Part (b): 96, 60, 48, 36 units; pearls the least
Part (c): Pandyas, pearls and naval power
Part (d): card chosen with a chapter-based reason

questions.q:
A water board in Tamil Nadu studies an old diversion structure on the Kaveri that now irrigates 3,00,000 hectares. Option 1: restore it again for Rs 40 crore, keeping 3,00,000 hectares. Option 2: replace it with a new barrage for Rs 110 crore, irrigating 3,30,000 hectares.
(a) Which king is credited with the old structure, and what is it called?
(b) What does the chapter say about its history of repair and its present use?
(c) Work out the extra land the new barrage would irrigate as a percentage of the present area, and the extra cost.
(d) Which option would you advise, and why?
questions.a: (a) Karikala; the Kallanai or Grand Anicut. (b) It was restored several times and is still in use, helping millions of people. (c) Extra land 30,000 hectares = 10% of 3,00,000; extra cost 110 - 40 = Rs 70 crore. (d) Either is acceptable if justified: restoring keeps a structure in use for centuries at lower cost; the barrage adds 10% more land but costs Rs 70 crore more.
s: Part (a): Karikala, Kallanai
Part (b): restored several times, still in use
Part (c): 10% and Rs 70 crore
Part (d): reasoned choice using both the chapter and the figures

questions.q: The Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha is named after Heliodorus, who was
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.134: it is named after an Indo-Greek ambassador whose inscription praises Vasudeva. The other roles belong to different people or periods of the chapter.

questions.q: Whom does the inscription on the Heliodorus pillar praise as the 'god of gods'?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.135 names Vasudeva. Shiva appears with the bull Nandi on a Kanishka coin, while Indra and Surya are mentioned in the Naneghat inscriptions.
o: Indra, the king of the gods

questions.q: The rule of the Indo-Greeks ended with the invasions of which people?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.135: the Shakas rose after the Indo-Greeks and stayed in power until the Kushanas arrived. The Kushanas are the tempting wrong answer because they came later.
o: The Kushanas, who came from central Asia

questions.q: Which statement about the Shaka Samvat is correct?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.135: it was developed in the Shaka period, is 78 years behind the Gregorian calendar (79 from January to March), and was adopted in 1957.
o: Behind the Gregorian year by 78 (79 in Jan-Mar)
Ahead of the Gregorian year by 78 all through the year
Adopted as the Indian National Calendar by the government in 1857
Developed by the Chola king Karikala for farm records

questions.q: Archaeologists find a silver coin in north India with a king on one side and Vasudeva-Krishna on the other. What does this best suggest about the issuer?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.135: some Indo-Greek coins depicted Indian deities like Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi, showing a blend of Greek and Indian elements. Kanishka's coins show the Buddha and Shiva; Satavahana coins show ships; Kharavela's record is an inscription.
o: A Kushana ruler like Kanishka had issued it
A Satavahana king had issued it for sea trade
Kharavela had struck it for Kalinga's use

questions.q: An official diary prints the date 20 February 2027 in the Gregorian calendar and also in the Shaka Samvat. Which Shaka year should it show?
questions.a: From January to March the Shaka Samvat is 79 years behind: 2027 - 79 = 1948. Using 78 gives 1949, a slip; adding gives 2105 or 2106, mistaking 'behind' for 'ahead'.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Some Indo-Greek coins show Indian deities like Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi.
Reason (R): The Indo-Greeks, though they arrived as conquerors, were much influenced by the rich local culture.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because they were influenced by local culture, they put Indian deities on their coins.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Indo-Greeks and Shakas.
1. The Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha was set up by Pushyamitra Shunga.
2. All Indo-Greek coins were made only of gold.
3. An official Government of India publication shown in the chapter gives dates in both the Gregorian and the Shaka Samvat eras.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: it is named after an Indo-Greek ambassador. Statement 2 is false: the coins were of gold, silver, copper and nickel. Statement 3 is true (Fig. 6.21).

questions.q: (a) Who were the satraps Alexander left behind, and what did they become? (b) Why were the north-western regions an easy target for them?
questions.a: (a) Regional rulers who set up independent domains and came to be known as Indo-Greeks. (b) After the decline of the Mauryas the northwest was weak.
s: Part (a): satraps who set up independent domains as the Indo-Greeks
Part (b): northwest was weak after the Maurya decline

questions.q: What does the inscription on the Heliodorus pillar say? Name the three 'immortal precepts' it mentions.
questions.a: It praises Vasudeva as the god of gods and says three precepts, when practised, lead to heaven: self-restraint, charity and consciousness.
s: Praise of Vasudeva as god of gods
Self-restraint, charity and consciousness

questions.q: (a) Name the four metals used for Indo-Greek coins. (b) What is shown on the two sides of a typical coin, and what showed a blend with India?
questions.a: (a) Gold, silver, copper and nickel. (b) A king on one side and Greek deities on the other; some coins instead showed Indian deities like Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi, showing the blend.
s: Part (a): gold, silver, copper, nickel
Part (b): king and Greek deities; Indian deities show the blend

questions.q: Compare the Indo-Greeks and the Shakas on two points: how each came to rule in the northwest, and what ended or limited its rule.
questions.a: The Indo-Greeks began as the satraps Alexander left behind, who set up independent domains; their rule ended with the invasions of the Shakas. The Shakas (Indo-Scythians) invaded the northwest, rose to power after the Indo-Greeks, and stayed in power until the Kushanas arrived.
s: How each came to rule: Alexander's satraps; the Shakas invading
What ended each: Shaka invasions; arrival of the Kushanas

questions.q: Who were the Shakas, and during which period did they rule in the northwest?
questions.a: The Shakas, also called Indo-Scythians, invaded the northwest and ruled from the latter part of the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE, after the Indo-Greeks and until the Kushanas arrived.
s: Identified as the Indo-Scythians who invaded the northwest
Rule from the latter 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE

questions.q: Sana says, 'We know most about the Indo-Greeks from their coins, and those coins show only Greek gods.' Which part is supported by the chapter, and which part is not?
questions.a: The first part is supported: coins found in north India give most of the information about these rulers. The second part is not: the coins often showed a king with Greek deities, but some depicted Indian deities such as Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supported: coins are the main source of information
Not supported: some coins show Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi

questions.q: A notice board shows the date 15 August 2026 with the Shaka year 2104. Use the chapter to show that the Shaka year cannot be right.
questions.a: From April to December the Shaka Samvat is 78 years behind the Gregorian calendar, so the year should be 2026 - 78 = 1948. The board's 2104 is 2026 + 78, which mistakes 'behind' for 'ahead'.
s: States the rule: 78 years behind
Calculates 2026 - 78 = 1948
Identifies the slip of adding 78 to get 2104

questions.q: Design a coin for an Indo-Greek king who wants to be accepted by both his Greek and Indian subjects. Describe each side and explain how the coin shows a blend of cultures.
questions.a: One side shows the king and the other a Greek deity; or one side shows the king and the other Vasudeva-Krishna or Lakshmi. The mix of Greek and Indian symbols shows a blend, as in real Indo-Greek coins.
s: A side with the king or Greek deity
A side with an Indian deity such as Vasudeva-Krishna or Lakshmi
Explains that the combination shows a blend of cultures

questions.q: 'The Indo-Greeks arrived as conquerors but became a part of India's cultural story.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Alexander's satraps became independent rulers called Indo-Greeks and took the weak northwest after the Mauryas. Though conquerors, they were influenced by the local culture, blending Greek and Indian elements in governance, art, language and daily life. Heliodorus, an Indo-Greek ambassador, praised Vasudeva as god of gods on the pillar near Vidisha. Their coins in gold, silver, copper and nickel sometimes showed Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi.
s: Origin as satraps and conquest of the weak northwest
Influence of local culture, blend in governance, art, language
Heliodorus pillar and its praise of Vasudeva
Coins with Indian deities
Conclusion linking conquest to cultural exchange

questions.q: Trace how rule in the northwest changed hands in this chapter, from Alexander's campaign in the Indus plains to the arrival of the Kushanas. Explain how each change became possible.
questions.a: Alexander left satraps behind while retreating; they set up independent domains as the Indo-Greeks. After the Mauryas declined, the weak northwest was an easy target for them. The Indo-Greeks were influenced by local culture. The Shakas invaded, ended Indo-Greek rule and stayed in power until the Kushanas arrived, probably in the 2nd century CE.
s: Alexander's satraps left behind
Satraps become independent Indo-Greeks
Weak northwest after the Mauryas made it an easy target
Shaka invasions end Indo-Greek rule
Kushanas arrive later, probably in the 2nd century CE

questions.q:
A museum card quotes the inscription on a pillar near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh, put up by an ambassador: 'the god of gods' is praised, and 'three immortal precepts, when practised, lead to heaven: self-restraint, charity, consciousness'.
(a) After whom is the pillar named, and whose ambassador was he?
(b) Whom does the inscription praise as the god of gods?
(c) What does the chapter say about the Indo-Greeks and the local culture they met?
(d) Two guides read the inscription differently. Guide 1: 'It shows that Heliodorus became a worshipper of Vasudeva.' Guide 2: 'It shows that an Indo-Greek respected an Indian belief.' Which reading can the chapter support better, and what extra evidence would Guide 1 need?
questions.a: (a) Heliodorus; an Indo-Greek ambassador. (b) Vasudeva. (c) They arrived as conquerors but were much influenced by the rich local culture, blending Greek and Indian elements. (d) Guide 2's reading is safer: the chapter says only that he praises Vasudeva and lists precepts. Guide 1 would need a statement that he took up the faith, and some coins also show Indian deities, which supports the blend but not his personal belief. Accept a reasoned case for Guide 1 using the praise.
s: Part (a): Heliodorus, Indo-Greek ambassador
Part (b): Vasudeva
Part (c): influenced by local culture, blending
Part (d): picks a reading and names the extra evidence needed

questions.q:
A museum catalogue lists 60 Indo-Greek coins found in north India. On 36 coins the reverse shows a Greek deity; on the other 24 the reverse shows an Indian deity, either Vasudeva-Krishna or Lakshmi. The curator must write one sentence for the display board.
(a) Which metals, according to the chapter, were used for Indo-Greek coins?
(b) What percentage of the 60 coins carries an Indian deity?
(c) What does the chapter say about the Indo-Greeks and the culture of the lands they entered?
(d) Sentence 1 reads 'The Indo-Greeks mostly kept to their own gods.' Sentence 2 reads 'The Indo-Greeks were much influenced by local culture.' Which would you prefer and why?
questions.a: (a) Gold, silver, copper and nickel. (b) 24/60 = 40%. (c) They arrived as conquerors but were much influenced by the rich local culture, blending Greek and Indian elements. (d) Either can be defended: 60% still show Greek deities, supporting sentence 1, but 40% with Indian deities and the chapter's statement support sentence 2, which fits the book more directly.
s: Part (a): gold, silver, copper, nickel
Part (b): 40%
Part (c): influenced by local culture, blend of elements
Part (d): a chosen sentence justified with data and chapter

questions.q: What title does the inscription on the headless statue give to Kanishka?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.136: 'mahaaraja rajadhiraja devaputra Kanishka'. Monk-king is Kharavela, 'god of gods' is how Heliodorus praised Vasudeva, and 'crowned kings' are the Sangam kingdoms.
o: The great king, king of kings, son of God
The monk-king, respector of every sect and temple
The great king, the god of gods, lord of all
One of the three crowned kings of the south

questions.q: Which stone was mostly used for sculptures in the Gandhara style?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.137: most Gandhara sculptures were crafted in intricate detail from grey-black schist. Red sandstone is the Mathura stone, and ivory and terracotta items appear in the Shunga collage.

questions.q:
Statement I: The Gandhara style grew in the Mathura region of present-day Uttar Pradesh.
Statement II: The Mathura style depicted only images of the Buddha.
Which option is correct?
questions.a: Gandhara emerged in western Punjab, and Mathura is in Uttar Pradesh. Mathura sculptors showed Kubera, Lakshmi, Shiva, Buddha, yakshas and yakshinis, so 'only' makes Statement II false.
o: Statement I is true, but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true.

questions.q: On Kanishka's coin showing the Buddha, in which script is the name of the Buddha written?
questions.a: Chapter 6 p.137: the Buddha is shown with the inscription BODDO in Greek script. Brahmi is the script of the other inscriptions in the chapter, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: A visitor sees a red sandstone sculpture of Kubera with a prominent moustache, a full figure and smooth modelling. Which school of art does it belong to?
questions.a: Red sandstone, fuller figures with smooth modelling and Indian deities mark the Mathura school (p.140). Kubera is the Mathura example in the chapter.

questions.q: A student sees one Kanishka coin with the Buddha and another with Shiva beside the bull Nandi, and says, 'He must have worshipped only one god.' What does the chapter's reading suggest?
questions.a: The chapter asks what putting Buddha and Shiva on coins says about the ruler's values; the Kushana sculptures also reflect the peaceful co-existence of various schools of thought. Jain devotion belongs to Kharavela and Vasudeva worship to the Satavahanas.
o: He made room for more than one faith
He followed Jain teachings, like Kharavela
He was a devotee of Vasudeva, like the Satavahanas
He gave land grants only to monks

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mathura sculptures show less influence of Greco-Roman aesthetics than Gandhara sculptures.
Reason (R): Mathura sculptures were carved mainly in red sandstone.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. The stone does not explain why the influence was less: the chapter gives the distinct Indian style as the reason, and the material is simply another difference.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Kushana age.
1. The Kushanas held no part of the Silk Route.
2. Deities such as Surya began to be shown in forms more like humans.
3. The composition of the Mahabharata and Ramayana is placed entirely before the age of reorganisation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the Kushanas held significant sections of the Silk Route. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says the period also saw their composition. Statement 2 is correct (p.137).

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its feature in Column B.
Column A: 1. Gandhara style  2. Mathura style  3. Kanishka's coins  4. The headless statue
Column B: a. Red sandstone and Indian deities  b. Buddha with Greek script; Shiva with Nandi  c. Inscription saying 'son of God'  d. Grey-black schist with Greco-Roman touches
questions.a: Gandhara: grey-black schist and Greco-Roman features; Mathura: red sandstone; Kanishka's coins: Buddha and Shiva; the statue: the 'son of God' inscription.

questions.q: (a) Where did the Kushanas originally come from, and how far did their empire stretch at its peak? (b) What did their hold on the Silk Route do for trade?
questions.a: (a) They came from central Asia; at their peak the empire extended from central Asia to large parts of northern India. (b) Trade grew, connecting India with other parts of Asia and the West.
s: Part (a): central Asia to large parts of northern India
Part (b): trade grew, linking India with Asia and the West

questions.q: Describe the two coins of Kanishka discussed in the chapter, one side of each.
questions.a: On the first, Kanishka holds a spear and is titled 'King of Kings', while the other side shows the Buddha with BODDO in Greek script. On the second, the emperor is on one side and Shiva with the bull Nandi on the other.
s: First coin: king with spear, Buddha in Greek script
Second coin: Shiva with Nandi

questions.q: (a) Name the two major epics the chapter says were composed in this period. (b) What does the chapter say about Sanskrit literature and about the themes that dominated the shared heritage?
questions.a: (a) The Mahabharata and the Ramayana. (b) Sanskrit literature flourished, and in the shared heritage Indian themes (especially Hindu and Buddhist ones) were dominant.
s: Part (a): Mahabharata and Ramayana
Part (b): Sanskrit flourished; dominance of Indian themes

questions.q: Name two deities shown in Mathura sculptures and two features of the figures made in the Mathura style.
questions.a: Deities such as Kubera, Lakshmi, Shiva, Buddha, yakshas and yakshinis. The figures are generally fuller, with smooth modelling.
s: Two correct deities
Fuller figures and smooth modelling

questions.q: State two changes in religious art during the Kushana age.
