questions.a: Representations of deities such as Surya looked more similar to humans, and religious art developed, laying the groundwork for later temple architecture.
s: Deities shown in more human-like forms, e.g. Surya
Growth of religious art that laid the groundwork for temples

questions.q: Leela says, 'Kanishka was a Buddhist ruler.' How far does the chapter support this? Give evidence for the part that is supported and the part that goes too far.
questions.a: Supported to a degree: one of his coins shows the Buddha with the name BODDO in Greek script. It goes too far if it means only Buddhism: another coin shows Shiva with the bull Nandi, and Kushana sculptures show many deities, reflecting peaceful co-existence of schools of thought.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supported: Buddha on a coin
Too far: Shiva with Nandi and many deities in sculpture

questions.q: A museum label reads 'Buddha statue, Mathura school, red sandstone', but the head is grey-black schist with realistic anatomy and flowing robes. Use the chapter to show that the label cannot be right.
questions.a: Mathura sculptures use red sandstone and show fuller, smoothly modelled Indian figures. Grey-black schist, realistic anatomy and flowing robes belong to the Gandhara style, which blended Greco-Roman and Indian features. So the label should read Gandhara school.
s: Material contradiction: schist is not Mathura's red sandstone
Realistic anatomy and flowing robes belong to Gandhara
Correct label: Gandhara school

questions.q: The chapter says this age should be viewed 'not as confined to any one kingdom or ruler, but as a dynamic process'. Explain what this means, using the Gandhara style as an example.
questions.a: It means the history was shaped by interaction and assimilation, not by one ruler. In the Gandhara style Greco-Roman elements blended with Indian features, under the Kushanas, showing cultures influencing one another.
s: Meaning: a process of interaction and assimilation over time
Gandhara example blending Greco-Roman and Indian features
Links it to cultural exchange rather than a single ruler

questions.q: Which of the three foreign peoples in this chapter, the Indo-Greeks, the Shakas or the Kushanas, changed life in the subcontinent the most? Defend your choice with two pieces of evidence and say what each of the other two added.
questions.a: A strong answer chooses one and supports it. Kushanas: control of significant sections of the Silk Route, so trade grew; the Gandhara and Mathura schools; Buddha and Shiva on coins; human-like deities that laid groundwork for temples. Indo-Greeks added a blend of Greek and Indian elements and coins with Indian deities, and the Heliodorus pillar. The Shakas added the Shaka Samvat calendar, developed during their period and adopted as the Indian National Calendar in 1957. Accept any consistent choice.
s: Chooses one people
First piece of evidence
Second piece of evidence
What one of the other two added
What the third added

questions.q: Compare the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art in terms of where they emerged, the stone they used, the influence on them, the subjects they showed and the look of the figures.
questions.a: Gandhara emerged in the western regions of Punjab; Mathura in the Mathura region of present-day Uttar Pradesh. Gandhara used grey-black schist; Mathura used red sandstone. Gandhara blended Greco-Roman elements with Indian features, while Mathura shows less Greco-Roman influence and has a distinct Indian style. Gandhara produced fine Buddha images with realistic anatomy and flowing robes; Mathura showed Kubera, Lakshmi, Shiva, Buddha, yakshas and yakshinis. Mathura figures are fuller with smooth modelling.
s: Regions of emergence
Stone used by each
Degree of Greco-Roman influence
Subjects depicted
Look of the figures

questions.q:
A museum has one display slot for Kanishka. Exhibit 1 is a massive headless statue, 1.85 m high, with an inscription in Brahmi script. Exhibit 2 is a pair of his coins, one with a spear-holding emperor and the Buddha, the other with an emperor and Shiva with the bull Nandi.
(a) What titles does the inscription on the statue give Kanishka?
(b) Name the two figures, besides the emperor, who appear on the coins.
(c) What does putting these two figures on coins say about his values, according to the chapter's questions?
(d) Which exhibit would you place in the slot, and what would you lose by leaving out the other?
questions.a: (a) Maharaja, rajadhiraja, devaputra: the great king, king of kings, son of God. (b) The Buddha and Shiva with the bull Nandi. (c) That a powerful ruler made room for more than one faith and valued their co-existence. (d) Either choice if reasoned: the statue shows how he saw his power through its titles; the coins show his values and his links, for example the Greek script on the Buddha coin. Leaving out the coins loses the evidence on faith; leaving out the statue loses the evidence of his claimed status.
s: Part (a): great king, king of kings, son of God
Part (b): Buddha and Shiva with Nandi
Part (c): co-existence of faiths, values of the ruler
Part (d): chooses an exhibit and says what the other would add

questions.q:
Class 7's role-play maps the Silk Route as 6,000 km from China to the Mediterranean, of which Kushana territory covered 1,800 km. Two captions are proposed. Caption 1: 'The Kushanas held significant sections of the Silk Route.' Caption 2: 'The Kushanas controlled the Silk Route.'
(a) What share of the route did the Kushanas hold, in percent?
(b) What did their hold on the route do for trade?
(c) How far did the Kushana empire extend at its peak?
(d) Which caption would you print? What extra figure about the route would you need before you could print the other?
questions.a: (a) 1,800 / 6,000 = 30%. (b) Trade grew, connecting India with other parts of Asia and the West. (c) From central Asia to large parts of northern India. (d) Caption 1 fits the chapter and the 30%; Caption 2 would need evidence that they held or commanded most of the 6,000 km, for example a share near 100%. A reasoned case for Caption 2 using their extent and influence is acceptable if it explains the 70% not held.
s: Part (a): 30%
Part (b): trade grew, connecting India with Asia and the West
Part (c): central Asia to large parts of northern India
Part (d): caption chosen and the extra figure named
